analysis.one_liner: Charges opioid makers a per-milligram fee to fund addiction treatment.
analysis.headline: A fee on opioid manufacturers to pay for addiction treatment never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress with 12 cosponsors and no action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged companies that make or import opioid painkillers one cent per milligram of active opioid sold. Money raised after rebates would flow to states to build and run addiction treatment programs and hire treatment workers in rural and underserved areas. Cancer and hospice patients, who legitimately need opioids, would be rebated so they don't pay the fee. The bill was introduced in March 2017, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People with opioid addiction who need treatment they can't get, especially in rural and medically underserved communities: the bill directs all net revenue to state treatment programs, new facilities, long-term residential care, housing and job support for people in recovery, and recruitment of treatment professionals. Cancer and hospice patients would also benefit, because the bill guarantees they pay nothing of the fee.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People seeking addiction treatment, especially in underserved areas

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 1-cent-per-milligram fee on sales of active opioids by manufacturers, producers, and importers, excluding drugs used to treat opioid addiction itself.

Requires every dollar of net new revenue to go to states exclusively for substance abuse treatment: new residential and outpatient facilities, sober living, long-term 30- to 90-day programs, housing and employment support for people in recovery, care for babies born with neonatal abstinence syndrome, and recruiting treatment providers for rural and underserved areas.
Establishes a rebate or discount program so cancer and hospice patients pay none of the fee, protecting pain patients who use opioids for legitimate medical reasons.
Requires HHS to report to Congress on whether the fee raised retail prices or hurt patient access, so the design could be corrected.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, producers, and importers of opioid painkillers would pay the fee directly. Some or all of it could be passed through to the retail price of opioids for other pain patients (not cancer or hospice, who are rebated), which is one of the things the bill's required report was designed to measure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Opioid manufacturers, possibly some other pain patients

drawbacks.text: A per-milligram fee is a blunt instrument: it raises the price of opioids across the board, not only in cases of overprescribing, and some patients with serious chronic pain outside cancer or hospice care would likely pay more at the pharmacy.

Companies may reduce supply or exit the market for low-dose or low-margin opioid products if the fee makes them unprofitable, potentially limiting access for patients who need them — another access concern the bill's mandated report was meant to track.

The rebate machinery for cancer and hospice patients adds administrative work for HHS and could be slow or burdensome to run, which the bill itself acknowledges by instructing HHS to minimize burden on patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was designed to make the industry responsible for a public health crisis partly rooted in over-marketed painkillers, and it anticipated the two strongest objections by rebating legitimate users (cancer and hospice patients) and requiring a report on price and access effects. The residual cost falls on some non-cancer chronic-pain patients and possibly on the availability of certain opioid products. The main treatment gap it addressed — lack of facilities and providers, especially rural — is real, and the funding mechanism was dedicated rather than discretionary.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2017 and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress; the committee never took it up and it never reached the Senate floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 2017 by Senator Manchin along with nine other Democratic and independent senators, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
Twelve senators cosponsored the bill: eleven Democrats and one independent.
The complete action history shows no further action after the referral to Finance — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers are better off because the bill never became law: they avoided a 1-cent-per-milligram charge on their products. The opioid epidemic's toll of untreated addiction continued to fall on families and state budgets instead of being partly shifted to the companies that sold the opioids.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who avoided the fee

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent King; no Republican senator signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.note: The bill put a 1-cent-per-milligram charge on every sale of active opioids, making the companies that profited from prescription opioids pay into treatment for the crisis those opioids fed. Because the bill died, they continue to sell without the charge.

Net revenue was earmarked for new treatment facilities, sober living homes, long-term residential programs, and recruitment of providers in underserved areas — funding that would have expanded a badly under-supplied sector. Providers' interest here runs with patients', since the bottleneck in opioid treatment is capacity and staffing.
Cancer and hospice patients were fully protected by a rebate program, but other pain patients could have faced higher pharmacy prices or reduced product availability from the fee.
